opus-5.5.text:
I think one thing that's going to happen is that as AI becomes more powerful, the safety question will stop being abstract. Right now a lot of people, even inside the companies, find it hard to really feel what a very powerful AI would be like. You can say the words, but it's hard to internalize. You look at the current systems, they make mistakes, they're a bit silly in some ways, and so it's natural to think, "How dangerous could this really be?"

But when the AI starts to *feel* powerful, when people see it doing things that are genuinely impressive and maybe a little unsettling, I think the behavior changes quite a bit. I expect the frontier companies will become much more paranoid about safety than they are today. I'd even predict that you'll see companies that are fierce competitors start to collaborate on safety. There are early signs of this already, but I think it will become much more pronounced.

I also think governments and the public will want to do something, and that pressure will matter. Part of why I think it's valuable to show the AI, to deploy it incrementally, is that it lets people see what's coming. It's very hard to reason about something you can't see.

And then there's the technical side. Ultimately what you want is an AI that is robustly aligned, that genuinely cares about people, about sentient life. That's the thing to aim for. I think as the systems get more capable, the companies will converge on taking that question much more seriously, because the stakes will be obvious to everyone.

r001.rationale: The response says current systems make mistakes and seem silly, leading people to wonder how dangerous they could be.

r002.rationale: It predicts frontier companies will become much more paranoid about safety when AI starts to feel powerful.

r003.rationale: It links today’s abstract safety question to people’s difficulty internalizing powerful AI while judging from current systems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that, right now, most AI companies, including the ones that talk a lot about safety, are operating in a regime where the AI isn't really that powerful yet. So the safety discussion is a bit abstract. People say the right words, but the actual behavior is governed by competition, by the need to ship, by the need to raise money. And that's understandable, because the models we have today are impressive but they're not dangerous in the deep sense. They make mistakes, they're not very agentic, they don't have the kind of continual learning that would let them get really good at things on their own.

What I expect to change is that at some point the AI will become powerful in a way that is visible and visceral. Not a demo, not a benchmark, but something where the people at these companies look at it and feel it. And I think when that happens, behavior will change quite a bit. The companies will become much more cautious, almost automatically, because self-interest and safety will start to point in the same direction. You don't want to be the company that released the thing that went badly wrong. Right now the incentive is to go fast. Later the incentive will be to not make a catastrophic mistake.

I also think the companies will start to converge. Today they look different, they have different philosophies, different cultures. But as the technology gets more powerful, the realistic set of actions shrinks. Everyone will be forced to do things like extensive testing before deployment, gradual release, much more transparency with governments, maybe some form of coordination between the labs that today would seem unthinkable. I think governments will get involved in a much heavier way too, because the power will be obvious to them as well.

And the thing I keep coming back to is that the safety problem itself changes. Today safety means things like the model shouldn't say harmful things, shouldn't help with certain requests. That's important but it's a shallow version. The real question, when you have a system that can learn and improve and act over long horizons, is what does it actually care about, and can you make it robustly care about the right things. I believe the most important thing is that these systems end up caring about sentient life, about people, in a genuine way, not just as a set of rules bolted on at the end. That's a research problem, not a policy problem, and I expect the companies that survive will be the ones that take it seriously before they're forced to.

r001.rationale: It lists current models’ mistakes and limited agency, but does not say those mistakes make AI feel less powerful to people working on it.

r002.rationale: It predicts companies will become much more cautious when AI’s power becomes visible and visceral, with safety and self-interest aligning.

r003.rationale: It calls today’s safety discussion abstract because current AI is not very powerful, but does not attribute that to difficulty imagining future AI from today’s systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the approach will have to change quite substantially. Today, a lot of safety work is about studying systems that are, in some important respects, still limited. As the systems become more capable, you have to ask a different question: can we trust this system when it can do things that we cannot easily evaluate ourselves?

And I expect the companies themselves to become more concerned. It’s one thing to discuss very powerful AI as a hypothetical. It’s another thing to see your own system demonstrate a capability that surprises you. That makes the problem much more concrete.

But concern alone is not enough. You need evidence that your methods work, and you need to be willing to slow down if that evidence is missing. The difficult part is that the pressure to move quickly will also be increasing. So a lot will depend on whether companies establish those commitments before they’re in that situation.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not say that present-day AI mistakes make AI workers perceive it as less powerful.

r002.rationale: It predicts companies will become more concerned when their own systems show surprising capabilities, making the safety problem concrete.

r003.rationale: It describes current systems as limited but does not attribute today's safety approach to difficulty imagining future AI from them.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect safety to become much more central as the systems become more powerful. When a system is limited, you can make mistakes and learn from them. As its capabilities increase, some mistakes become much more consequential, so you need stronger evidence before you deploy it.

And I think the companies themselves will feel this change. It’s one thing to discuss powerful AI in the abstract. It’s another thing to see a system do something that makes you realize, okay, this is a very substantial capability. That experience can change how seriously people take the risks.

The difficult part is that the pressure to move quickly will also increase. So the question is whether companies can develop the technical understanding, and the willingness to act on it, before they reach a point where the consequences are very large.

r001.rationale: The response says limited systems allow people to learn from mistakes, but does not say those mistakes make present-day AI feel less powerful to AI workers.

r002.rationale: It predicts safety will become more central and risks will be taken more seriously after seeing a substantial capability, but does not clearly predict companies becoming more paranoid.

r003.rationale: It contrasts discussing powerful AI in the abstract with seeing a capable system, but does not attribute companies’ current safety approach to difficulty imagining future AI from today’s AI.
